doc.title: Luis Conte interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 24, 2025

title: First recordings: Camilo Azuquita single and a failed TV session
summary: His first recording was a 45 with singer Camilo Azuquita where he first overdubbed; his first studio call, for a TV show hosted by Leonard Nimoy, went badly because he played too busy.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Did you have a similar memorable experience with your first studio date? I mean you described your first paying gig really well. And do you recall the first time someone said we want you to record? You go, “Ooh, what’s that?”

Well my very first, first, first, first recording was with a Cuban Latin band, a salsa band you call now, it was with Camilo Azuquita he was a singer from Panama, of Cuban descent, that moved to L.A. and it was actually my first cool salsa gig in L.A. way, way, way back. And he wanted to record a 45, back in those days there were 45s, two songs. And I was the conga player in the band. And I went to the studio, I’d never been in a studio, I’d never seen this. And I realized that I play the congas and we needed somebody to play guiro, we didn’t have a guiro player. I said, “I’ll do it.” And I played over the track I had just played, you know, that thing that – I didn’t know you could do that.

Yeah. Overdub. So I overdubbed the guiro and then I overdubbed the maracas. And I went like, “I want to do this.” I love this. Yeah. That was my first experience man with Azuquita. But, so here’s the next thing though, so I had seen the recording studio. Now I’m going man, I hope somebody calls me for a session. You’re networking, “Here’s my number, man” you know blah-blah-blah. And I got a call, unfortunately I don’t remember who these guys were, but I got a call, it was for a TV show. It wasn’t a good experience, a TV show that was Journey to the Unknown or something like that, with Leonard Nimoy. It was a short – it didn’t last long that show. Leonard Nimoy was the host and he would talk about these weird things, supernatural things, whatever. And I get called, “Yeah we need somebody to play congas – can you bring some congas” you know. So I brought my congas and it was this experience of the red light went on and I played what I thought was cool, and they didn’t dig it. And they said it was either two busy or, I just, I froze man. I literally froze. I didn’t know what to do. So I wasn’t sure what to try to do so I just tried something else. That didn’t work out. Then we’d do it again, it didn’t work out. They said, “Okay, well thanks so much, Luis” you know. They gave me a check, “Really appreciate it man, thank you. Bye.” “Okay thanks, bye.” I get in my car, I’m driving out as I’m driving out I see another percussionist come in. It just broke my heart. So there is good experiences and bad experiences. I got nailed. So then I tried to find out what happened you know. And I called my buddy. So the guy that was coming in was a friend of mine, his name was Hector El Grade, who has passed now. And we called him Bucky. We became really, really good friends. We were already really good friends and I called him the next day I said, “Hey man I saw you coming into the studio, I was totally bummed out I just left, I was crying.” I said, “What happened, I don't know, did you do

that session?” He goes, “Yeah, yeah they just wanted this thing and you’ve just got to play simpler man.” He told me, “Man, this is not Cuban music. They didn’t want that. They wanted –” I went, “Oh.” So I just focus in and do it.
Sometimes the producers – if they don’t know the music they may have a hard time telling you what they want but when you play it, “Oh yeah, that’s what we want” but I can’t tell you.

That could have been it. And that’s probably, yeah. Because hindsight much later, now that I’ve had lots of experience recording I walk in a studio and I can tell if this guy knows what the hell’s going on or not. And I know how to play ‘em. I totally know how to turn them around and play ‘em. I’m not mentioning names but man there’s some guys that you think that would know, they have no idea. And you know a great producer really calls you because by now they know what you do and they let you do what you do you know. And they’re open to your ideas. And once you play, sometimes maybe you played something that they don’t dig and they may say, “Hey maybe try a different pattern” or “maybe that’s a little too busy” or something. Or maybe, “Do you have a different instrument?” But they let you come in and do your thing.
